To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the following variables were associated with instability in spinal metastasis: tumor size, magnitude and direction of spinal loading, tumor location, and bone density.

the following are the risk factors for instability of the spine: increased tumor size; a larger cross-sectional defect; increased force of spinal load; decreased bone density; posterior location of the tumour within the vertebra; destruction of the costoveebral joint; pedicle destruction in thoracolumbar vertebra; increased axial rigidity; sagittal spinal deformities.
instability and impending instability of thoracolumbar metastatic disease are multifactorial and that there is a need for further clinical research to determine the best predictors of instability.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the instability of the thoraco-lumbar spine with spinal metastasis and the risk factors associated with this instability.
the biomechanical and clinical issues of metastatic disease of thoracolumbar vertebrae.
defining the criteria of instability in patients with spinal tumors and the risk factors for instability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the risk of instability in patients with spinal tumor is dependent on a variety of factors including tumor location, tumor size, tumor type, bone density, magnitude of spinal load, and sagittal deformity.
the definition of instability in the spine is a combination of the above factors, which is yet to be determined.

the following are risk factors for impending instability in patients who have spinal metastases: 1) a tumor size of > 50% of the cross-sectional area of the vertebral body, 2) destruction of the pedicle and/or posterior vertebral body, and 3) destruction of the costotransverse or costovertebral joints.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
instability of the spine in metastatic disease occurs when the forces applied to the spine are greater than the strength of the remaining bony and ligamentous support.
instability in spinal metastasis is defined as a condition of the spine that is not able to tolerate the normal physiologic loads and movements in daily life.
instability of the spine in patients with metastases is a dynamic process that is dependent on multiple factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a need for a consensus on what is instability, what is impending instability, and what are the risk factors for instability.
there is a lack of high-quality research to guide the surgeon in identifying instability in patients with spinal involvement from metastatic disease.
the current literature is not adequate to make recommendations for the surgical management of patients with spinal metastasis.
